question_text: Why is instantaneous speed a limit of averages?
audio_script: Your speedometer says fifty. Over what? The last second? The last minute? Each window gives a different average. The dial is claiming something stronger — the speed right now. But at an instant, no time passes and no distance accumulates. So what is the dial actually measuring? Here is the trick. Pick any interval, compute the average speed. Shrink the interval. Compute again. Keep shrinking. If the averages settle toward a single number, that number is the instantaneous speed. On a position-versus-time graph — Ohanian calls it the worldline — the average speed is the slope of the secant line connecting two points. As the interval shrinks, the secant pivots. In the limit, it becomes the tangent. The instantaneous speed is the slope of that tangent. This is the derivative. Newton and Leibniz invented calculus because they needed this idea to be precise. Every speed dial is a derivative in disguise. The worldline tells you where something has been. Its tangent tells you where it is going, right now, in the only sense physics can define right now. Everything in kinematics is built on this single limiting idea.

question_text: Why do beginners add a force that does not exist?
audio_script: Here is the single most common mistake in introductory mechanics. A block is sliding on a rough floor. You draw the free-body diagram. You include the weight, the normal force, the friction. And then you add one more arrow — pointing in the direction of motion — because the block is moving, so something must be pushing it. That arrow does not exist. Newton's second law says accelerations come from forces. Not the other way around. A block sliding at constant velocity on a rough floor has zero net force. Its motion is not a force. Its motion is not a cause. Motion is what happens when forces balance, or when they do not. This is Newton's first law, and it is easy to forget in the middle of a problem. When you build a free-body diagram, ask two questions. First, what is touching the object? Every contact gives a force. Second, is there a long-range force — gravity, or an electric charge? Draw only those. Then, and only then, set the vector sum equal to mass times acceleration. If the block is accelerating, the diagram will show you which force caused it. If the block is not accelerating, the arrows must cancel. The rule from Ohanian's study guide is simple and it is worth writing on your hand: forces cause acceleration. Accelerations do not cause forces.

header_title: When Friction Gives Instead of Steals
question_text: Why is friction sometimes a source of kinetic energy?
audio_script: You have heard that friction always robs energy. That is only half true. Friction between two surfaces at the same temperature always dissipates mechanical energy into heat. But the work done by friction on a *chosen object* can be positive or negative. Consider a block sitting on a conveyor belt. The belt is moving, the block is at rest relative to the ground. Friction grabs the block and drags it forward. On this block, friction does positive work. On the belt, friction does negative work. Neither of those statements contradicts the other. Ohanian's general work-energy theorem separates the bookkeeping: start with potential and kinetic energy, add the work from all nonconservative forces, and end with potential and kinetic energy at the new position. If the net nonconservative work is positive, mechanical energy grows. If negative, it shrinks. The theorem does not care whether the nonconservative force is called friction, tension, or a push. It only cares about the sum. On a rough floor, when the block is being dragged, friction is your enemy. On a conveyor belt, when the block is being caught up, friction is your friend. The physics is the same; the sign comes from the problem you set up. So the next time someone tells you friction always removes energy, ask them where the block is sitting.

header_title: The Falling Elevator Is the Universe
tagline: Weight and gravity are locally indistinguishable
question_text: Why can no experiment tell free fall from deep space?
audio_script: You are standing on a bathroom scale. The building you are in snaps its cable. You fall. The scale reads zero. Your weight has not changed. Your mass is the same. Gravity still pulls you down. But you and the scale are accelerating downward at g, so there is no normal force left for the scale to measure. Here is the twist Ohanian's study guide is careful to point out. The same scale reading — zero — could also be obtained by removing you and the scale to deep space, far from any mass, and letting the whole apparatus drift. Free fall and weightlessness are locally indistinguishable. This is Einstein's equivalence principle, and it is the seed of general relativity. The word is local. If your body is very large, the gravitational field varies from your head to your feet, and tidal effects give you away. But for a small lab in free fall, the physics inside is exactly the physics of empty space. This is why astronauts float on the space station. They are not far from Earth's gravity. They are falling around it, forever missing the ground. And inside their little falling room, no experiment — pendulum, laser, gyroscope — can tell them whether they are at rest in the void or crashing toward a planet.

tagline: Every firework has a still center
question_text: Where is the center of a spinning
audio_script: [{"type":"momentum_exchange","id":"collision","mass1":1.0,"mass2":3.0,"v1":4.0,"v2":0.0,"color":"#4CC9F0"},{"type":"dot","id":"cm","pos":[-0.5,0.0,0.0],"color":"#F1C40F","label":"CM"}]
orientation: Light a firework and it explodes into a hundred pieces flying in every direction. Every piece follows its own chaotic trajectory. But watch a single point — the center of mass — and something amazing happens. That point continues along the smooth parabola it would have followed if the firework had never exploded. It does not know the firework broke apart. This is the heart of Ohanian's chapter on systems of particles. Newton's second law, applied to every atom, is a nightmare of bookkeeping. But apply it once to the center of mass and it becomes simple: the net external force equals total mass times the acceleration of the center of mass. Internal forces — the gunpowder pushing the shell fragments apart — cancel in pairs by Newton's third law. They never move the center of mass. This is why a bullet and a rifle recoil together. Why a rocket accelerates even though the exhaust is pushing away from it. Why two ice skaters who push off each end up with the same center of mass they started with. A hundred particles, a thousand, a billion. The center of mass always behaves like a single particle carrying all the mass, driven by the net external force. Every explosion has a still point. The center of mass knows nothing of chaos.

tagline: Distribution of mass sets the race
question_text: A hoop and a disk roll down the same hill. Which is first?
audio_script: Take a hoop and a solid disk, same mass, same radius. Put them at the top of the same ramp. Release. The disk reaches the bottom first. Every time. Why? Both lose the same gravitational potential energy. Both end up with the same total kinetic energy. But kinetic energy comes in two flavours: translational, one-half m v squared, and rotational, one-half I omega squared. For rolling without slipping, v equals omega R, so the rotational share depends only on the moment of inertia. The hoop's mass sits at the rim, far from the axis. Its moment of inertia is m R squared. The disk's mass is spread out, with much of it closer to the axis. Its moment of inertia is only one-half m R squared. So a bigger fraction of the hoop's kinetic energy goes into spinning, and less is left for moving forward. The hoop is slower. The same physics explains why a hollow sphere loses to a solid sphere, and why a can of soup rolls faster than an empty can. It is not the mass that matters. It is where the mass lives. Ohanian makes this point with a flywheel: almost all its moment of inertia is in the outer rim. That is the design. That is the engineering lesson hiding inside a physics formula.

header_title: Push the Swing at the Right Time
question_text: Why does a tiny push build to a huge swing?
audio_script: Push a child on a swing. Push at the wrong moment — say, when the swing is coming toward you — and the swing slows down. Push at the right moment — just as it starts to fall away — and a small effort builds a huge arc. This is resonance, and it is one of the most powerful ideas in physics. A driven oscillator has a natural frequency, the rate at which it wants to swing. Push at that frequency and the amplitude grows. Push far from it and nothing much happens. The sharpness of this peak is measured by a number called Q, the quality factor. High Q means a very sharp resonance. A tuning fork has a Q in the thousands. A car's suspension has a Q of a few. Low Q systems respond over a wide range of frequencies; high Q systems respond strongly but only near the sweet spot. Ohanian's study guide frames Q as a measure of ringing time: how many radians the system oscillates through before the amplitude decays to one over e of its value. A high Q oscillator rings for a long time. A low Q oscillator dies quickly. Every radio, every microwave oven, every MRI machine uses resonance to select a single frequency from a sea of noise. And every child on a swing already knows the physics intuitively.

question_text: Why does heat flow one way and never the other?
audio_script: Put a drop of ink in a glass of water. Stir. The ink spreads through the water, evenly, and it stays that way. Now try to reverse it. Try to get all the ink molecules to gather back into a single drop, in the corner of the glass. You cannot. Not because the laws of mechanics forbid it. Every collision between ink and water is reversible. If you ran the movie backward, every collision would still obey Newton's laws. But the number of ways to arrange the ink molecules so they are all in one corner is astronomically smaller than the number of ways to arrange them so they are spread out. The system evolves toward the more numerous arrangements, not because it is forced to, but because it is overwhelmingly more likely. This is entropy. Ohanian's chapter frames it as a measure of disorder, but the better word is multiplicity. The number of microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic appearance. Second law of thermodynamics: in an isolated system, entropy never decreases. Not because the reverse is forbidden, but because it is so improbable that you would need to wait longer than the age of the universe to see it. Drop ink into water. Watch it spread. That is not a law. That is a statistical near-certainty.

question_text: Why does a dielectric reduce the electric field?
audio_script: You charge a parallel-plate capacitor to some voltage and disconnect the battery. The plates hold their charge. The electric field between them is set. Now slide a slab of plastic between the plates. The field shrinks. Not by a little — by a factor that depends on the plastic. For ordinary plastic, the factor is three. For certain ceramics, it can be thousands. Where does the field go? It does not go anywhere. It gets cancelled, partially, by the plastic itself. Every molecule inside the plastic is either a permanent electric dipole, or it becomes one when placed in a field. These dipoles align with the applied field. Their positive ends point one way, their negative ends the other. They create a bound surface charge on the faces of the slab, and that bound charge produces a field that opposes the original field. The net field inside the plastic is weaker than the field in vacuum. Ohanian calls the ratio the dielectric constant, kappa. It is a property of the material. The capacitor's capacitance rises by the same factor, because the charge on the plates is unchanged but the voltage has dropped. This is why real capacitors have dielectrics inside. Not just to keep the plates apart, but to multiply the capacitance for free.

header_title: Magnetism Is Just Electricity in Disguise
question_text: Why do moving charges attract even when they have the same sign?
audio_script: Two parallel wires carry current in the same direction. They attract. This is strange. Both wires contain moving electrons, and like charges repel. So why do the wires pull together? Ohanian's study guide gives the deep answer, and it is one of the most beautiful arguments in physics. Take the rest frame of the moving electrons inside one wire. From that frame, the other wire is not neutral. The positive ions in the other wire are moving backward, and length contraction packs them closer together. The electrons in the other wire are also moving, but at a different speed, so their spacing changes by a different amount. The net effect is a charge imbalance. A charge imbalance means an electric field. And an electric field pulls. What we call magnetism in the lab frame, an observer riding on the electrons calls electricity. Same force, different accounting. The mathematics comes out clean: the magnetic force is the electric force multiplied by v squared over c squared. It is a relativistic correction to Coulomb's law. Magnetism is not a separate force. It is electricity viewed from a moving frame. That is why the speed of light appears in Maxwell's equations, and why an electric motor and a moving charge are the same physics.

header_title: How Many Meters in a Furlong?
question_text: A furlong is one-eighth of a mile. How many meters?
audio_script: A furlong is one-eighth of a mile. One mile is sixteen hundred nine meters. So one furlong is sixteen hundred nine divided by eight, which is two hundred one meters. The closest answer is two hundred. Answer C. This is a straightforward conversion, but it is worth remembering that historical units still show up in horse racing and in old land surveys. The furlong, the chain, the rod — all still defined, all still in use.

header_title: Average Speed Is Not the Simple Average
question_text: A jogger runs 2 km at 10 km/h then walks 2 km at 6 km/h. Average speed?
audio_script: A jogger runs two kilometers at ten kilometers per hour. Then she walks two kilometers at six kilometers per hour. What is her average speed for the whole four kilometers? The tempting answer is eight — the average of ten and six. That answer is wrong. Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Time running is two over ten, which is zero point two hours. Time walking is two over six, which is zero point three three hours. Total time is zero point five three hours. Four divided by zero point five three is seven point five. Answer A. The answer is closer to the slower speed because more time was spent there. This is called the harmonic mean, and it shows up whenever you average rates.

question_text: Vector A is 10 units west. Vector B is 5 units at 70° N of E. Resultant?
audio_script: Two vectors. A is ten units due west. B is five units at seventy degrees north of east. Find the resultant. Use the law of cosines. The angle between them, taken tip to tail, is one hundred ten degrees. R squared equals ten squared plus five squared minus two times ten times five times cosine of seventy degrees. That is one hundred plus twenty five minus one hundred times zero point three four two. Which gives ninety. The square root of ninety is approximately nine point five. Answer A. The law of cosines works because vector addition is the same as triangle geometry, just dressed in different notation.

header_title: Can the Man Catch the Bus?
question_text: A man runs 6 m/s toward a bus 15 m away. Bus accelerates at 1 m/s². Does he catch it?
beats_json: A man runs at six meters per second toward a bus that is fifteen meters away. As he starts to run, the bus begins to accelerate at one meter per second squared. Does he catch it? Set up the equations. The man's position is six t. The bus's position is fifteen plus one-half t squared. Set them equal. Six t equals fifteen plus zero point five t squared. Rearrange. Zero point five t squared minus six t plus fifteen equals zero. Use the quadratic formula. t equals three point five seconds, or t equals eight point four seconds. Both are valid mathematically. But the man only needs the first one. He catches the bus at three point five seconds, and if he keeps running, he will pass it — then at eight point four seconds, the bus catches up to him. Answer A, at three point five seconds.

tagline: A bullet embeds in a block
question_text: A 20g bullet at 300 m/s embeds in a 500g block. Speed of block?
audio_script: A twenty gram bullet is fired at three hundred meters per second into a stationary five hundred gram block. The bullet embeds. What is the speed of the block just after? Momentum is conserved because the collision is very fast compared to any external forces. Before. Zero point zero two times three hundred equals six kilogram meters per second. After. The combined mass is zero point five two kilograms. Divide. Six over zero point five two is eleven point five meters per second. Answer B. Notice that kinetic energy is not conserved. Before, nine hundred joules. After, only about thirty four joules. The rest went into deforming the block and heating it. This is why ballistic pendulums are used to measure bullet speeds.

header_title: How Close Can an Alpha Get?
question_text: An 8 MeV alpha approaches a gold nucleus (Z=79). Closest approach?
audio_script: An eight mega-electron-volt alpha particle is aimed directly at a gold nucleus. How close does it get? An alpha has two protons. Gold has seventy-nine protons. Set the initial kinetic energy equal to the electric potential energy at the closest approach. Eight MeV is eight times ten to the sixth electron volts. That is one point two eight times ten to the minus twelve joules. The Coulomb constant times two times seventy nine times the square of the electron charge is three point six four times ten to the minus twenty six. Divide. Closest approach is two point eight times ten to the minus fourteen meters. Answer A. That is well outside the nuclear radius of gold, which is about seven times ten to the minus fifteen meters.

question_text: A proton at 0.99999c crosses a 10^5 ly galaxy. Proper time?
audio_script: A proton travels at zero point nine nine nine nine nine c across the Milky Way. One hundred thousand light years in the galaxy's rest frame. How much time elapses on the proton's own clock? The Lorentz factor is one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. For v equals zero point nine nine nine nine nine c, that is roughly three hundred sixteen. Proper time is coordinate time divided by gamma. One hundred thousand years divided by three hundred sixteen is about four hundred fifty years. Answer A. The proton crosses a hundred thousand light years of space in four hundred fifty years of its own time. From the proton's point of view, the galaxy is contracted — not a hundred thousand light years across, but about three hundred twenty light years. It never breaks the speed of light. It just takes a shortcut through spacetime.

tagline: Why red light cannot eject electrons
question_text: Potassium has a work function of 2.0 eV. Threshold wavelength?
audio_script: A potassium surface has a work function of two point zero electron volts. What is the longest wavelength of light that can eject an electron? Use Einstein's photoelectric equation. At the threshold, the photon's energy exactly equals the work function. h c over lambda equals phi. Solve for lambda. Six point six three times ten to the minus thirty four, times three times ten to the eighth, divided by two point zero times one point six times ten to the minus nineteen. That is six point two four times ten to the minus seven meters. Answer A, six hundred twenty four nanometers. That is deep red. Longer wavelengths — infrared — cannot eject electrons from potassium, no matter how bright. This is why Einstein's photon model replaced the wave model of light. Brightness does not matter; only frequency.

question_text: A 20g bullet at 300 m/s embeds in a 500g block. CM kinetic energy?
audio_script: A twenty gram bullet embeds in a five hundred gram block. We found the block moves at eleven point five meters per second. What is the kinetic energy of the center-of-mass motion? The combined mass is zero point five two kilograms. The center-of-mass velocity is eleven point five meters per second. Kinetic energy is one half times zero point five two times eleven point five squared. That is thirty four joules. Answer A. But before the collision the total kinetic energy was nine hundred joules. Where did the other eight hundred sixty six joules go? Into internal energy of the block — heat, deformation, sound. In the center-of-mass frame, all that energy was internal. The bullet was moving relative to the center of mass, and that relative motion is what got dissipated. This is the deepest way to think about collisions, and Ohanian's study guide is clear about it.

question_text: What is the escape velocity from Earth's surface?
audio_script: What speed do you need to leave Earth and never come back? Set the kinetic energy equal to the gravitational binding energy. One half m v squared equals G M m over R. The m cancels. v equals the square root of two G M over R. G is six point six seven times ten to the minus eleven. M is five point nine eight times ten to the twenty four kilograms. R is six point three seven times ten to the sixth meters. Plug in. v is eleven point two kilometers per second. Answer B. That is about twenty five thousand miles per hour. Not quite as fast as a satellite in low orbit, which needs only seven point nine kilometers per second — but that satellite never escapes. The escape speed is the orbital speed times the square root of two. This is why the Moon does not have an atmosphere: its escape speed is too low to hold on to gas molecules.
